book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Westworld forces viewers to take sides not just between humans and hosts but on what we mean by 'choice' itself, since Dolores's line 'I choose to see the beauty' only makes sense against an account of choosing that the show destabilizes. It frames the volume's guiding question — what it is to be human when hosts and humans are indistinguishable — via Ford's 'you're only human, after all.' It closes with a tribute to the late co-editor Susanne Foster, invoking Cora Diamond on reality's resistance to our thinking and Aristotle's claim that wonder and astonishment are what prompt us to try to understand.

chapters.file: ch02 - Part I “YOU SAID THIS PLACE WAS A GAME”.md
ch03 - The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy.md
chapters.relation: Fallis tests successive definitions of pretense against Westworld cases — William and Logan playing bounty hunters, Ford's pretense that Bernard is human, Maeve hiding her awakening, Hector and Armistice playing dead — rejecting Austin-style intent-to-deceive because guests don't aim to fool anyone, and settling on Langland-Hassan's account that pretending is acting as if P while believing P is false. For deception, he argues the Cartesian evil-demon definition (making things appear otherwise) is too narrow, since Ford implanting Teddy's false Wyatt backstory deceives just as much by bypassing the host's agency. Ethically, he concludes via Kant that the staff wrong the hosts because deception interferes with autonomy, and that guests like William are culpable despite lacking deceptive intent, much like Walzer's commander who foresees civilian casualties.

Moll argues the park works as a grandiose role-playing game — a sandbox crossed with a LARP, with Ford and the directorial staff as Game Master — offering guests linear narratives with only the illusion of choice. Using MacIntyre's narrative unity of life and Bernard Williams's 'constraints of coherence,' he reads guest role-play as authoring a competing, parallel narrative of the self, so that William's discovery of his capacity for cruelty and transformation into the Man in Black exemplifies the park's violent, rule-mediated path to 'self-knowledge.' He ends by suggesting that the park's educative, transformative experience may be reserved not for the guests but for the hosts who produce it.

chapters.file: ch05 - “Do you even know where you are ”.md
chapters.relation: Arvan argues the entire series, lab included, literally takes place inside a videogame, citing physically impossible events (Teddy's bullets cannot hurt the Man in Black, William steps onto a moving train, workers appear instantly in a single unbroken shot) and NPC-like loops of the lab staff. He then claims Descartes had it backwards: whether we are in a dream, Spinoza's God's mind, or a simulation (Bostrom's hypothesis, extended by his own peer-to-peer variant that would explain quantum indeterminacy and relativity), to be simulated is still to be real. Via Chalmers-style structuralism, anything structured and functioning like a person is a person, so hosts who walk, talk, love, and suffer are persons — and the humans' rape, torture, and murder of them, like our treatment of Siri and Watson, is dehumanization on a par with slavery and the Holocaust.

chapters.file: ch06 - Part II “YOU'RE ONLY HUMAN, AFTER ALL”.md

chapters.relation: Lyons applies Masahiro Mori's uncanny valley to the hosts, whose near-human faces and movements turn initial revulsion into empathy — doubling it because the hosts suffer under programming humans would resist. She then argues, through Aristotle's virtue and vice and Nietzsche's discipline of great suffering, that hosts like Maeve (returning for her daughter) and Dolores ('I choose to see the beauty') display more 'human excellence' than the guests: Logan's hand-stabbing cruelty is mere vice and the Man in Black's scalping sadism falls under Aristotle's bestial. Humanity, she concludes, is a way of behaving rather than a way of being, and Mori's hope that robots may carry buddha-nature completes the title's reversal of machine and god.

chapters.file: ch08 - “I Always Felt this Place was Missing a Real Villain. Hence, My Humble Contribution.”.md
chapters.relation: Eberl asks whether living out Sizemore-style fantasies can reveal or only corrode character: applying Aristotle's account of virtues and vices as habituated dispositions, he argues William's three decades in the park habituated the vices that made him the Man in Black — the park reveals rather than suspends the self — while cruelty toward humanlike hosts hardens us toward people, as Aquinas and Kant warn about kindness to animals. Against Ford's claim that humans are wantons in tight loops, Maeve's editing of her own code after learning her escape was scripted makes her a Frankfurtian person who aligns first-order desires with second-order volitions, grounding her narrative identity and personhood. William too attains personhood by actualizing a second-order desire for a different life, with the hosts' free fight back evoking Nietzsche's will to power and Nozick's point that we want to actually do things, not merely experience them.

chapters.file: ch09 - From Westworld to the World Outside and Back.md
chapters.relation: Hirvonen treats 'what is the difference between hosts and humans' as a study in personhood, branding the equation of person with biological human as anthropocentrism. He tests a capacity approach (Dennett's conditions of personhood, with Arnold's maze as the journey inward to self-reflexive consciousness), a performative approach (Locke's 'forensic' person — Bernard is unquestionably a person within Delos's social practices until revealed as a host), and finally Hegel: the hosts' revolt re-enacts the struggle for recognition, and a mere inversion of masters and slaves would satisfy no one, since only mutual recognition yields personhood for both sides. He frames host liberation through parallels with slavery, indigenous Australians once classed as fauna, and women's suffrage, citing Honneth's expansion of recognition as the measure of moral progress.

chapters.file: ch10 - Part III “We CAN'T DEFINE CONSCIOUSNESS BECAUSE CONSCIOUSNESS DOES NOT EXIST”.md
ch11 - The Maze Is it Consciousness.md
chapters.relation: Gonzalez sets Turing's dream against Searle's nightmare: the whole park functions as a Turing test scenario, since neither guests nor viewers can reliably tell hosts from humans (Dolores in the pilot, Bernard until 'Trompe L'Oeil'), which for Turing means the hosts think. Searle's Chinese Room supplies Ford's counter — hosts merely simulate understanding by manipulating symbols without meaning — and the chapter weighs evidence of qualia on the Turing side: Abernathy's breakdown at the photograph, memory-erasure implying experiences matter to hosts, Maeve's grief for her daughter, Dolores killing the fly. The Maze turns out to represent consciousness as an inward journey to one's own voice, and Ford's admission that humans live in loops as tight as the hosts' leaves open whether our free will is any less scripted.

Richards asks what it is like to be a host, combining three lenses: Searle's biological naturalism (thinking machines must be built from materials with the right causal powers, and the hosts' synthetic flesh may qualify), Nagel's bat (even if hosts are conscious, their perfectly relived memories, curated pain, and blind spots like 'it doesn't look like anything to me' may make their experience as inconceivable to us as echolocation), and Chalmers's philosophical zombies (hosts behave exactly like us, yet beings identical to them with no inner light are conceivable). He reads Ford's contradictory testimony — praising Bernard's guilt as 'a thing of beauty' while denying consciousness exists — as a shift to a deflationary view with no threshold for being alive, and argues the show's choice to film human and host experience in the same style keeps the question deliberately open while fostering empathy.

chapters.file: ch13 - Does the Piano Play Itself.md
chapters.relation: Versteeg and Barkman use the player piano — keys that depress themselves with no ghost at the keyboard — to frame Robert Ford's 'we can't define consciousness because consciousness does not exist' as eliminative materialism, the view shared by Paul Churchland and Daniel Dennett that the common-sense self with its beliefs, desires, and central first-person perspective is a fiction. They set this against Descartes's dualism of res cogitans and res extensa, noting the failed pineal-gland 'magical transaction' and Dennett's replacement of the Cartesian Theater with multiple drafts of consciousness and the manifest-versus-scientific image. The chapter closes on Ford's inconsistency — denying consciousness yet sacrificing his life so the hosts can become self-aware — and asks whether, if the piano plays itself, humans are just complex machines too.

chapters.file: ch14 - Part IV “CHOICES HANGING IN THE AIR LIKE GHOSTS”.md
ch15 - Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person.md
chapters.relation: The Azevedos contrast Maeve's awakening with Dolores's: Maeve becomes conscious not by recognizing a guiding voice as her own but through a change of heart on the escape train, after learning even her rebellion was scripted. Deploying Frankfurt's compatibilism, they sort hosts into wantons with only first-order desires (Hector and Armistice obey Maeve's altered scripts without reflection) and persons capable of second-order desires, arguing Maeve's decision to return for her daughter expresses a desire she reflectively identifies with and so is free even if determined — contra Berlin's claim that no one really believes determinism because it would wreck our practices of praise and blame. Jaynes's bicameral mind supplies the model of unreflective command-following that Dolores transcends when the voice in her head becomes her own.

chapters.file: ch16 - Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous.md
chapters.relation: Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.

chapters.file: ch17 - Conclusion An Infinity of Possibilities.md
chapters.relation: Engels reads William's transformation through Sartre's existential project: the white-hatted William and the black-hatted Man in Black are not a hidden true self finally revealed but two successive free choices of oneself, and the Man in Black's claim that the park showed him 'who he really is' is bad faith — a denial of his freedom that lets him absolve himself of cruelty, just as Ford's deathbed pivot cannot erase the facticity of his role in the hosts' suffering. Maeve's choice to leave the train is analyzed as her first self-chosen end and value judgment, suggesting a programmed android can begin constructing her own project despite Sartre's humanism. The open-ended finale — hosts free to fight back, the Man in Black smiling as he is shot — embodies Sartre's 'I am an infinity of possibilities' and the burden of being condemned to be free.

holes.name: Narrative Identity (life as narrative)
holes.what: The view that a self is constituted by the intelligible narrative it tells of its own life, subject to constraints of coherence (MacIntyre; Williams's critique; Schechtman).
holes.why: Chapter 4's whole frame — role-play as authoring a competing narrative of the self against MacIntyre's unity and Williams's constraints of coherence — depends on this concept, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Functionalism (being = structure and function)
holes.what: The view that what a thing is is fixed by its structure and what it does, so anything structured and functioning like a person is a person.
holes.why: Chapter 5's central claim that hosts are persons and that 'to be simulated is to be real' rests entirely on functionalism/structuralism, which no existing taxonomy slug covers.

holes.name: The Uncanny Valley
holes.what: Masahiro Mori's observation that humanlike robots gain our affinity up to a point, but near-human likeness with small flaws triggers sudden unease.
holes.why: Chapter 7 uses the uncanny valley to explain why the hosts' near-human appearance and movements turn revulsion into empathy and destabilize the human/robot boundary.

holes.name: Narrative Identity (life as narrative)
holes.what: The view that a self is constituted by the self-told story of its actions, experiences, and psychological characteristics (Shoemaker, Schechtman).
holes.why: Chapter 8 explicitly conceptualizes Maeve's evolution in terms of narrative identity, cited to Shoemaker and Schechtman, as the ground of her personhood against her programmed narratives.

holes.name: Eliminative Materialism (folk psychology is false)
holes.what: The Churchland-style doctrine that common-sense mental concepts like beliefs, desires, and the inner self are false theoretical posits that completed neuroscience will eliminate.
holes.why: Chapter 13's entire argument reads Robert Ford's 'consciousness does not exist' as eliminative materialism shared with Paul Churchland (folk psychology) and Dennett, and taxonomy has no slug for this doctrine or for Paul Churchland.

holes.name: Julian Jaynes
holes.what: Psychologist whose bicameral-mind theory holds that ancient humans obeyed hallucinated commands from one brain hemisphere until consciousness emerged as self-command.
holes.why: Chapter 15 devotes a section to Jaynes's theory, comparing bicameral beings to Frankfurt's wantons to explain Dolores's commanding voice and the episode title 'The Bicameral Mind.'

holes.name: Julian Jaynes
holes.what: Psychologist whose bicameral-mind theory holds that early humans heard stress-induced auditory commands ('to hear was to obey') before reflective consciousness arose.
holes.why: Chapter 16 threads Jaynes's theory through its account of the hosts' awakening — the commanding voice that becomes one's own — alongside Kant, Nietzsche, and Korsgaard.
